records.description: Yoneichi Matsuda, from a Vashon Island strawberry farming family, volunteers from Heart Mountain internment camp to serve in the U.S. Army's legendary 442nd Regimental Combat Team.
records.details: While interned at Heart Mountain War Relocation Center in Wyoming, Yoneichi Matsuda -- whose family had farmed strawberries on Vashon Island since 1927 -- volunteered to serve in the U.S. Army's 442nd Regimental Combat Team. The 442nd was composed almost entirely of Japanese American men and became the most decorated unit for its size and length of service in U.S. military history, fighting in the European theater against Nazi forces. His sister Mary Matsuda later described his departure from camp as one of the saddest days of the family's life. Mary herself would eventually leave the camps to join the U.S. Cadet Nurse Corps.

records.title: Partial Return of Japanese Americans to Vashon
records.description: Only about one-third of Vashon's exiled Japanese Americans return to the island after the war; many find their property lost or destroyed.
records.details: After the war ended and the camps were closed, only about one-third of the 111 Japanese Americans forcibly removed from Vashon on May 16, 1942, returned to the island. Many families had lost all their belongings except what they could carry in two suitcases. Some learned that homes belonging to Japanese residents had been burned during the war. Political hostility toward returning Japanese Americans in Washington State discouraged others from coming back. The Sakaharas, for example, chose not to return and rebuilt their lives elsewhere. The Mukai family did return from self-exile in Oregon, reopened their home and garden, resumed strawberry farming, and restarted their cold-process fruit barreling plant. The once-thriving Japanese American farming community on Vashon was permanently diminished.

records.title: Washington State Ferries Begins Service
records.description: Washington State Ferries takes over island ferry service on June 1, 1951, replacing the private Vashon Ferry System.
records.details: After the private Vashon Ferry System operated for three years, Washington State Ferries assumed control of the route on June 1, 1951. This transition brought the island into the state transportation network. Around this time, state officials proposed connecting Vashon-Maury Island to the mainland with bridges, but islanders increasingly opposed the idea, fearing it would destroy the island's rural character and invite urban sprawl.

records.title: Nike Missile Base S-61 Established on Vashon Island
records.description: The U.S. Army establishes Nike missile site S-61 on Vashon Island as part of a twelve-site defense ring protecting Seattle during the Cold War.
records.details: In 1953, as Cold War fears of Soviet atomic attacks on Seattle grew, the U.S. Army deployed the 513th Air Defense Battalion's Battery C ('Charlie Battery') on Vashon with anti-aircraft guns. Between 1956 and 1957, the government purchased land through eminent domain for three sites: Sunrise Ridge (administration and fire control), Paradise Ridge (missile launch area with underground silos), and Oakwood Terrace (housing). The base was designated S-61 in the twelve-site Metropolitan Defense Ring surrounding Seattle. Initially armed with Nike Ajax missiles, the site was upgraded to Nike Hercules in June 1960 -- one of only three Seattle-area bases to receive the more powerful missiles. The 433rd Anti-Aircraft Artillery Missile Battalion, Battery A, operated the base until its closure in 1974. The Sunrise Ridge site, ironically, had been a strawberry farm owned by the Matsumoto family before the government condemned the land.

records.title: Vashon Bridge Proposal Defeated in State Legislature
records.description: A bill to fund a bridge connecting Vashon Island to the mainland dies in the Washington State Senate after Lt. Governor John Cherberg's procedural ruling, effectively killing the most serious bridge proposal in island history.
records.details: By the late 1950s, the Washington Toll Bridge Authority had advanced an ambitious plan to build a cross-sound highway: a floating bridge from Fauntleroy to Vashon (which would have been the largest floating structure ever built at 11,666 feet), a superhighway across the island, and a suspension bridge across Colvos Passage to the Kitsap Peninsula. Engineers estimated 3-4 million vehicle crossings in the first year, with construction costs of approximately $100 million. On March 12, 1959, after the state legislature struggled for nearly three months during a second special session, the House passed the appropriations bill. However, Lt. Governor John Cherberg, who served as Senate president, ruled that the House bill had broadened the original scope and must return to committee. A vote to override Cherberg's ruling failed 21 to 28. The bill died in the Highways Committee and the bridge was never built. Opponents included the Pilots Association, the Port of Tacoma, and Eastern Washington legislators, along with a growing number of Vashon residents who feared becoming 'another Mercer Island.'

records.title: Vashon Allied Arts Becomes Oldest Private Nonprofit Arts Organization in Washington
records.description: Vashon Allied Arts (formerly the Vashon Arts League, founded 1949) receives its 501(c)(3) nonprofit status, becoming the oldest private nonprofit community arts organization in Washington State.
records.details: The Vashon arts community traces its institutional roots to 1949, when island artists Fred Eernisse, Norman Edson, and Art Hansen formed the Vashon Arts League to show art created by islanders. After moving through several temporary homes -- the Lisabuela schoolhouse and the Cove Road Church -- the organization was revitalized by Shirley Speidel and others who found a home in the old Boy Scout Cabin at Ober Park. In 1966, the organization received 501(c)(3) status under the name Vashon Associated Arts, making it the oldest private nonprofit community arts organization in the state. The organization would eventually become Vashon Center for the Arts (VCA), growing into the island's largest nonprofit with programs in visual arts, performing arts, arts education, and dance.

records.title: Counterculture Influx Transforms Vashon Island
records.description: An estimated 200-700 counterculture migrants settle on Vashon Island during the Boeing Bust era, fundamentally reshaping the island's cultural identity.
records.details: The Boeing Bust and economic downturn of the early 1970s created an opening for counterculture and alternative-lifestyle individuals to find affordable housing on Vashon. As island families left to seek employment, small abandoned farms became available at low rents. By 1971, an estimated 200-700 'hippies' lived on the island alongside about 6,500 existing residents. A planned Memorial Day Weekend Rock Festival in Paradise Valley in 1970 sparked community tensions -- three loggers held down and forcibly cut the hair of 17-year-old Tony Grant, shops posted 'No Shoes, No Shirts, No Service' signs, and some called for an armed 'Sheriff's Deputy Auxiliary' to control the supposed invasion. Over 700 people attended a hearing and shouted down the armed patrol idea. Cannabis cultivation became widespread, earning Vashon the lasting nickname 'Weed Island' for the high-quality 'Vashon Gold' strain sold across the West Coast. Despite early friction, the counterculture movement permanently transformed Vashon from a quiet agricultural community into the progressive, arts-oriented enclave celebrated by the bumper sticker 'Keep Vashon Weird.'

records.title: The Bike in the Tree: Vashon's Accidental Landmark
records.description: A child's red bicycle left in the woods by Don Puz in 1954 is gradually absorbed by a growing fir tree, becoming one of Vashon Island's most iconic and quirky landmarks.
records.details: In 1954, the Puz family suffered a devastating house fire that killed Don Puz's father and destroyed all their possessions. In true 'Vashon fashion,' neighbors donated household items to help the family rebuild, including a red bicycle for young Don. At some point, Don left the bicycle leaning against a small fir tree in the woods near what is now Vashon Highway SW and SW 204th Street, behind the building called Sound Food. Over the decades, the tree grew around the bicycle, gradually absorbing it into the trunk. The sight became a beloved local attraction and the inspiration for Berkeley Breathed's children's book 'Red Ranger Came Calling.' A widely circulated but false internet story claims the bike belonged to a boy who left it to fight in World War I and never returned. Jeff Ammon, who owned Vashon's only bike shop, maintained the landmark by replacing handlebars and wheels when vandals stripped them. Don Puz, who grew up to become a King County Sheriff's deputy, confirmed his ownership when he returned to see the tree decades later.

records.title: Island Resists Bridge Construction
records.description: Vashon Island residents successfully resist repeated proposals to build a fixed bridge to the mainland, preserving the island's rural isolation.
records.details: Over several decades, various proposals to connect Vashon Island to the mainland via bridge were debated and ultimately rejected. Islanders recognized that a bridge would fundamentally alter the character of their community, making it a suburb of Seattle rather than a distinct island community. The ferry-dependent isolation became a defining and deliberately preserved feature of island life.

records.title: K2 Corporation Founded on Vashon Island
records.description: Brothers Bill and Don Kirschner found K2 Corporation on Vashon Island, pioneering fiberglass ski technology that revolutionizes the ski industry.
records.details: Bill Kirschner, a University of Washington engineering graduate, had been experimenting with fiberglass skis in his grandfather Otto's garage on Vashon Island since the 1950s while running Kirschner Manufacturing, which produced veterinary splints and research cages from fiberglass. After years of prototypes that broke apart during testing at Crystal Mountain, Bill perfected a wet-wrap fiberglass process in 1961. In 1962, he and brother Don formally founded K2 -- named for both the world's second-highest mountain and the two Kirschner brothers. Only 250 pairs shipped in 1964, but by 1967 the business was separated from Kirschner Manufacturing, and by 1968, K2 was selling 21,000 pairs annually with 83 employees. The company's racing program brought instant success with U.S. Ski Team adoption. At its peak, the Vashon factory employed approximately 750 islanders, making K2 the largest private employer on the island.

records.title: K2 Sports Manufacturing on Vashon
records.description: K2 Sports operates a major ski and sporting goods manufacturing facility on Vashon Island before eventually moving production to China.
records.details: K2 Sports was one of Vashon Island's largest employers, manufacturing skis and other sporting equipment on the island for decades. The company's eventual decision to move manufacturing to China represented a significant economic shift for the island, as it lost one of its few major industrial employers. Similarly, Seattle's Best Coffee operated a roastery on the island until it was acquired by Starbucks and the operation was closed.

records.title: Stewart Brothers Coffee Opens Roastery on Vashon Island
records.description: Jim Stewart moves his coffee roasting operation to Vashon Island, establishing the roastery that would become Seattle's Best Coffee.
records.details: In 1982, coffee entrepreneur Jim Stewart moved his roasting facilities to Vashon Island, purchasing a historic building constructed from old-growth island fir in the town of Vashon. The building featured an expansive covered porch, high ceilings, wooden floors, and an underground cellar perfect for storing rare coffee beans. Stewart had started in the coffee business in 1969 with the Wet Whisker ice cream and coffee shop on Whidbey Island. After winning first place in a regional coffee tasting competition judged by the area's top chefs, the company changed its name from Stewart Brothers Coffee to Seattle's Best Coffee (SBC). The Vashon roastery became the birthplace and production center for one of the Pacific Northwest's most iconic coffee brands. Starbucks acquired SBC in July 2003 and closed the Vashon facility on October 23, 2003, moving production to their Kent, Washington roastery. The historic building was later reopened as The Vashon Island Coffee Roasterie, still roasting coffee with the original equipment.

records.title: Vashon Island Farmers Market Established
records.description: The Vashon Island Growers Association (VIGA) establishes a farmers market, sparking a revival of sustainable agriculture on the island.
records.details: In the mid-1980s, a group of islanders formed the Vashon Island Growers Association (VIGA) with the goal of creating on-island farming jobs. They started a small farmers market near the Post Office and joined Washington Tilth, a statewide organization promoting local organic agriculture. By 1990, the market moved to its current site at the Village Green. In 1998, VIGA received a grant to build a permanent shed structure, and the following year led a community-wide effort that raised over $200,000 to purchase the Village Green property. The market became a catalyst for the fifth stage of island agricultural history: a revival of sustainable and organic farming methods after decades of agricultural decline following the WWII internment and postwar economic shifts. VIGA also developed educational programs including a horticulture curriculum at Vashon High School. The Saturday market now runs April through October, featuring farm produce, local crafts, prepared foods, and live music.

records.title: Vashon-Maury Island Land Trust Founded
records.description: Islanders establish the Vashon-Maury Island Land Trust to preserve natural areas, beginning with the purchase of Whispering Firs Bog.
records.details: In 1989, a dedicated group of islanders concerned about preserving Vashon's natural character informally organized to purchase Whispering Firs Bog, a fragile and unique wetland ecosystem near the Episcopal Church. The organization formally incorporated in 1990 as the Vashon-Maury Island Land Trust. Since its founding, the Land Trust has permanently protected over 2,000 acres of land, built 10 miles of public trails, and preserved key natural features including salmon-bearing streams, major ponds, diverse forests, and shoreline areas. Notable preserves include Shinglemill Creek, Judd Creek, Fisher Pond, and Christensen Pond. The Land Trust also permanently protected the remaining 12 acres of the historic Matsuda Farm, linking conservation with Japanese American heritage preservation. The organization launched programs like 'Seven over Seventy' to conserve large private holdings and 'The Four Creeks Campaign' to protect the island's major watersheds. Vashon carries half of all King County's shorelines, giving the Land Trust an outsized role in Puget Sound aquatic habitat protection.

records.title: Mukai Farm Listed on National Register of Historic Places
records.description: The Mukai Farm and Garden on Vashon Island is listed on the National Register of Historic Places, preserving one of the last intact pre-WWII Japanese American farmsteads in America.
records.details: In 1993, the Mukai house, Japanese garden, and cold-process fruit barreling plant -- along with the five acres remaining of the original 60-acre farm -- were designated a King County Landmark. The following year, 1994, the site was included on the National Register of Historic Places. The property was founded by Issei pioneer B.D. (Denichiro) Mukai in 1926 as a strawberry farm. The Japanese garden was designed and installed in the 1930s by Kuni Mukai, a Japanese immigrant woman -- making it the only known Japanese garden of that era designed by a woman. The nonprofit Friends of Mukai maintains the property as a heritage site and cultural center, hosting the annual Japan Festival, Day of Exile commemorations, and public tours. The 'Nisei Trilogy,' a collaborative artwork by poet Lawrence Matsuda and artist Roger Shimomura depicting the Japanese American wartime experience, is on permanent display in the Mukai house.

records.title: Glacier Northwest Gravel Mine Controversy on Maury Island
records.description: A 13-year battle over Glacier Northwest's proposed gravel mine expansion on Maury Island ends when King County purchases the 200-acre site for $36 million, creating a new county park.
records.details: Glacier Northwest had operated a gravel mine on the southern tip of Maury Island since the 1940s. In 1998, the company announced plans to dramatically expand operations to approximately 7.5 million tons of gravel per year, including construction of a 305-foot pier for barge transport. The proposal ignited fierce community opposition led by Preserve Our Islands, a grassroots organization founded by Sharon Nelson. Environmental concerns included arsenic contamination from decades of ASARCO smelter fallout, threats to an aquatic reserve surrounding the site (one of only four in Washington), potential harm to endangered Southern Resident orca whales from barge noise, and drinking water contamination. Over 500 islanders rallied at Gold Beach in one of Vashon's largest protests. After Glacier Northwest won multiple legal battles and began pier construction, a federal judge blocked further work in 2009, ruling the Army Corps of Engineers had acted 'arbitrarily and capriciously' in violation of the Endangered Species Act. On December 30, 2010, King County Executive Dow Constantine completed the purchase of the site for $36 million, funded through the Asarco settlement, Conservation Futures fund, and a CalPortland lease extension. The parcel became a county park, protecting a mile of shoreline and over 200 acres of madrone forest adjacent to the 320-acre Maury Island Regional Marine Park.

records.title: K2 Sports Moves Manufacturing Off Vashon Island
records.description: K2 Sports relocates manufacturing from Vashon Island to Guangdong, China in 2001, and moves its business offices to Seattle's Industrial District in 2006, ending over 40 years on the island.
records.details: In 2001, facing pressure to remain financially competitive in a globalizing market, K2 Sports moved its manufacturing operations from Vashon Island to Guangdong, China. At its peak, the Vashon factory had employed approximately 750 local people, making K2 one of the island's largest private employers. On June 22, 2006, K2 announced it was also relocating its business offices from Vashon Island to Seattle's Industrial District. The original factory building on Vashon Highway remained vacant for over a decade until its sale in July 2018 to Sound Properties, LLC. The departure of K2 represented a significant economic blow to Vashon, accelerating the island's transition from a place with industrial employment to primarily a residential and arts community.

records.title: Mary Matsuda Gruenewald Publishes 'Looking Like the Enemy'
records.description: At age 80, former Vashon Island resident Mary Matsuda Gruenewald publishes her memoir of wartime internment, preserving the story of the island's Japanese American community.
records.details: Mary Matsuda Gruenewald, born on Vashon Island in 1925 to Japanese immigrant strawberry farmers Heisuke and Mitsuno Matsuda, published 'Looking Like the Enemy: My Story of Imprisonment in Japanese American Internment Camps' in 2005. The memoir recounts her family's forced removal from Vashon on May 16, 1942, and her experiences at the Pinedale Assembly Center, Tule Lake, and Heart Mountain camps. It also tells the story of her brother Yoneichi's service with the 442nd Regimental Combat Team and her own enlistment in the U.S. Cadet Nurse Corps. David Guterson, author of 'Snow Falling on Cedars,' described it as 'a painfully honest narrative of imprisonment.' A Young Readers edition was published in 2010. In 2017, Vashon Island High School retroactively awarded Gruenewald the diploma she was denied when internment cut short her education. She died on February 11, 2021, at age 96. The memoir is now widely used in university and high school curricula.

records.title: Vashon Island COVID-19 Community Response
records.description: Vashon Island mounts a volunteer-led pandemic response that achieves the lowest COVID-19 case rate in King County, earning national recognition as a model for rural communities.
records.details: When the Seattle area became the nation's first COVID-19 hotspot in March 2020, Vashon Island faced unique vulnerabilities: an older-than-average population (median age 53), no hospital, limited clinic capacity, and ferry-dependent access to testing and medical care. Unemployment on the island quickly reached 22%, with four out of ten businesses going dark. The Vashon Medical Reserve Corps (VMRC) and VashonBePrepared launched an integrated response program that included community education (200+ situation reports, bilingual English-Spanish materials), free SARS-CoV-2 testing (7,500+ PCR tests), rapid contact tracing (560 index cases investigated), and an aggressive vaccination campaign (19,000+ doses delivered in partnership with Vashon Pharmacy). A community fundraising drive raised $325,000, later supplemented by $413,000 in government reimbursements. Volunteers contributed over 31,500 hours, and the relief fund subsidized over 4,400 bags of groceries and 28,000 meals. Over the first 22 months, Vashon achieved the lowest cumulative COVID-19 case rate in King County: 11.2 cases per 1,000 residents versus the countywide 49.6. The New York Times recognized VMRC's approach as a model for rural and tribal communities. A peer-reviewed study published in PLOS ONE confirmed the response's effectiveness.

records.title: sx̌ʷəbabš (Sqababsh / S'Homamish)
records.description: Original permanent inhabitants of Vashon and Maury Islands. Built five main village sites. Relied on salmon fishing, shellfish, hunting, and plant harvesting. Descendants are enrolled members of the Puyallup Tribe of Indians.

records.title: Julie K. Stein
records.description: Co-edited the publication "Vashon Island Archaeology: A View from Burton Acres Shell Midden" (2003), documenting the collaborative excavation of the Burton Acres Shell Midden site after a 1995 storm exposed its contents.

records.title: Laura S. Phillips
records.description: Co-edited "Vashon Island Archaeology: A View from Burton Acres Shell Midden" (2003) with Julie K. Stein, publishing the findings from the 1995 excavation involving 375 volunteers.

records.title: Judy Wright
records.description: Contributed to the collaborative excavation and study of the Burton Acres Shell Midden on Quartermaster Harbor, which documented centuries of indigenous habitation.

records.title: Manuel Quimper
records.description: Sailed the Princesa Real into the Strait of Juan de Fuca in 1790, discovering Admiralty Inlet -- the entrance to Puget Sound -- but did not enter. First European to report seeing Mount Baker.
records.period: Active on the Strait of Juan de Fuca in 1790

records.title: Juan Carrasco
records.description: Identified the entrance to Admiralty Inlet (leading to Puget Sound and the waters around Vashon Island) during the 1790 Spanish expedition, though the expedition did not proceed south into it.

records.title: Francisco de Eliza
records.description: Ordered both the 1790 Quimper expedition and the 1791 Narvaez expedition to explore the Strait of Juan de Fuca. The 1791 expedition passed by Admiralty Inlet but did not enter Puget Sound, leaving it for British discovery the following year.

records.title: Jose Maria Narvaez
records.description: Passed by Admiralty Inlet in 1791 aboard the Santa Saturnina but returned to Nootka Sound without exploring Puget Sound, leaving the waterway for George Vancouver's expedition the next year.

records.title: Captain George Vancouver
records.description: Named Vashon Island after his friend Captain James Vashon during British surveys of Puget Sound. Produced the first European maps of the area.

records.title: Captain James Vashon
records.description: The island's namesake. A fellow naval officer and friend of George Vancouver.

records.title: Peter Puget
records.description: Led a week-long survey of the southern Puget Sound in two rowing craft, passing Vashon Island and charting the waterway's farthest inlets. Vancouver named the southern portion of the waterway "Puget's Sound" in his honor on May 29, 1792.
records.period: Active on Puget Sound in May 1792

records.title: Joseph Whidbey
records.description: Accompanied Peter Puget on the week-long survey of southern Puget Sound, departing HMS Discovery on May 20, 1792, and sailing past Vashon Island while charting the waterway.
records.period: Active on Puget Sound in May 1792

records.title: William A. Maury
records.description: Maury Island's namesake. The smaller island adjacent to Vashon was named after him when Lt. Wilkes charted the waters of Puget Sound in 1841.

records.title: Lt. Charles Wilkes
records.description: Named Maury Island after crew member William A. Maury. Named Quartermaster Harbor and nearly all of Vashon-Maury Island's coastal points after quartermasters on his voyage. First American survey of the area.

records.title: Archibald McDonald
records.description: Established Fort Nisqually in 1833, the first European settlement on Puget Sound, near the mouth of Sequalitchew Creek. The fort served as a fur trade hub and drew European and American attention to the broader Puget Sound region, including Vashon Island.

records.title: Samuel Royal Thurston
records.description: Authored the Donation Land Claim Act of 1850, which granted up to 640 acres of Oregon Territory land to married settlers. The act provided the legal mechanism under which Vashon Island was later claimed, starting in the 1860s. It explicitly excluded Black and Hawaiian settlers.

records.title: Isaac Stevens
records.description: Negotiated the Medicine Creek Treaty of 1854, which ceded indigenous lands to the U.S. government and led to the removal of the S'Homamish from Vashon Island. His treaty terms provoked the Puget Sound Indian War of 1855–1856.

records.title: Chief Leschi
records.description: Led resistance against the Treaty of Medicine Creek's unfair terms during the Puget Sound Indian War of 1855–1856. Retreated east after the Battle of Seattle (January 26, 1856), was later captured, controversially convicted of murder, and hanged in 1858. Posthumously exonerated in 2004.

records.title: John Swan
records.description: Served as guard over nearly 5,000 indigenous men, women, and children -- including the S'Homamish from Vashon Island -- who were forcibly interned on Fox Island during the Puget Sound Indian War. Over one-third of the internees fell ill under devastating conditions.

records.title: Andrew J. Pope
records.description: Together with William C. Talbot, filed the first formal land claim on Vashon Island on August 1, 1864 -- 80 acres on the west side of the island for logging operations. Both were from Maine sawmill families.

records.title: William C. Talbot
records.description: Together with Andrew J. Pope, filed the first non-indigenous land claim on Vashon Island in 1864. Their Port Gamble mill had been operating since 1853, and the Vashon claim expanded their timber operations throughout Puget Sound.

records.title: Arthur Phinney
records.description: Made land claims totaling 592 acres on Vashon Island in 1864, the same year Pope and Talbot filed their claim. His claims encompassed the area that would later become the town of Vashon.

records.title: Mathew Bridges
records.description: First permanent homesteader, marking the beginning of European-American settlement on the island.

records.title: Salmon Sherman
records.description: Along with his wife Eliza Sherman, settled along Quartermaster Harbor in 1877, taking shelter in an abandoned logger's shack they nicknamed "Fort Necessity." Considered the first permanent family settlers. Descendants, now in their sixth generation, still live on the island.

records.title: Eliza Sherman
records.description: Settled with her husband Salmon Sherman along Quartermaster Harbor in 1877. Part of the first permanent family settlement on Vashon Island, arriving with the Price and Gilman families from Minnesota.

records.title: S.D. Sherman
records.description: Established the first semi-regular ferry service to Vashon Island by converting a lifeboat into the schooner Old Black Joe. Previously rowed mail from Tacoma to Quartermaster Harbor. Served as an essential transportation link for the growing island community.

records.title: T.D. Soper
records.description: Petitioned King County for Road No. 117 (today's SW Bank Road), leading from the island's center to the brickyard and post office at Vashon Landing. This was among the first official county roads on the island.

records.title: Edwin Broadway
records.description: Petitioned King County for Road No. 116 (today's SW Cemetery Road), running from the center of the island to the Ellisport dock. One of the first official county roads established on Vashon Island.

records.title: Mason Holmes
records.description: Petitioned King County for Road No. 118 (today's Vashon Highway SW), running south from Road No. 117. This road became one of the island's most important transportation arteries.

records.title: Samuel C. Herriott
records.description: Served as the first postmaster when the Vashon Post Office opened on April 12, 1883, establishing an official U.S. government presence and regularizing mail delivery on the island.

records.title: Albert Atwood
records.description: Organized the first Methodist class on Vashon Island on April 4, 1884, leading to the construction of the island's first church building the following year.

records.title: John N. Dennison
records.description: Sent Rev. Albert Atwood to organize a Methodist class on Vashon Island in response to requests from island residents, initiating the establishment of the island's first church.

records.title: R.B. Dilworth
records.description: Organized the first Chautauqua assembly on Puget Sound, held at Dilworth Point on Vashon Island on August 3, 1885. Had been active in the original Chautauqua assembly in New York since 1874. Dilworth Point is named after him.

records.title: John F. Vanderhoef
records.description: Took command of the steamer Iola in 1887 and established six weekly round trips between Tacoma, Seattle, and Vashon Island landings, creating the island's first reliable Mosquito Fleet connection. Held the mail contract for the east side of Vashon-Maury Island.

records.title: Lucian Cook
records.description: Ran a brickyard on Quartermaster Harbor, bought the steamer Estella to transport bricks and workmen to Tacoma, and later commissioned six barges and purchased the steamer Seaside as a towboat. Key figure in the island's brick manufacturing boom that supplied Seattle and Tacoma.

records.title: Frank Gorsuch
records.description: Built and opened the first store at the crossroads that became the town of Vashon in 1890. His general store, which still stands, effectively founded the town of Vashon. The building was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2000.

records.title: Ira Thompson
records.description: Recalled that "although overland travel was tough and the mud deep, Gorsuch was soon doing business with people throughout the Island," providing firsthand testimony about the founding of the town of Vashon.

records.title: Miles F. Hatch (also Miles Hatch)
records.description: Founded and named the town of Burton after his birthplace. Donated the hilltop campus land for Vashon College and spearheaded its founding in 1892. Operated a sawmill at Assembly Point, developed the Mileta Farm dairy, and built a store at the Burton Peninsula. Burton became the island's dominant town under his leadership.

records.title: A.C. Jones
records.description: Hired as the first president of Vashon College at Burton, which opened in 1892 as a non-denominational Christian co-educational institution offering classical and scientific programs, a pharmacy school, conservatory of music, and school of commerce.

records.title: John Cage Gorsuch
records.description: Planted the first commercial strawberry operation on Vashon Island in the early 1890s. By 1896, he was harvesting 6,120 pounds per acre from his three-acre farm, launching the island's signature agricultural industry that would ship 120,000 crates annually by 1909.

records.title: Howard C. Stone
records.description: Built the two-story Burton Masonic Hall for the Woodmen of the World fraternal order in 1894, the island's first fraternal building. The hall is now a designated King County landmark.

records.title: J.E. Mace
records.description: Discovered bags of smuggled opium on a Vashon Island beach in 1895 and reported his find to the Seattle Customs Office. Received $175 by court order for turning in the opium, revealing the island's position along Pacific Northwest maritime smuggling routes.

records.title: Asa Start
records.description: Neighbor of J.E. Mace, on whose property Mace buried smuggled opium found on the beach in 1895 before reporting it to government authorities.

records.title: J.T. Thompson
records.description: The first telephone line on Vashon Island ran half a mile between the local newspaper office and the J.T. Thompson household in 1891 -- little more than an acoustic wire system.

records.title: Frances Sherman
records.description: Ran a sawmill in Paradise Valley and won a contract to supply lumber for the Luna Park amusement park at Alki Point. Part of the island's active lumber industry during the growth era.

records.title: Helmar Steen
records.description: Founded the Steen Mill and built a logging railroad along what is now Cove Road. His mill provided his home with an early luxury -- electric light -- before the island's formal electrification in 1913.

records.title: Mark Twain
records.description: Reportedly among the notable speakers at the Puget Sound Chautauqua Assembly at Tramp Harbor on Vashon Island, which featured a 1,200-seat pavilion and drew audiences from across the region.
records.period: Reportedly spoke at Vashon Chautauqua, late 1800s–early 1900s

records.title: Theodore Roosevelt
records.description: Reportedly among the notable speakers at the Puget Sound Chautauqua Assembly at Tramp Harbor on Vashon Island, reflecting the assembly's national cultural significance.
records.period: Reportedly spoke at Vashon Chautauqua, early 1900s

records.title: Denichiro Mukai
records.description: Developed a renowned strawberry barreling method that concentrated flavor and moisture. Built a cold-process fruit barreling plant in 1926. His farmstead, listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1994, is now a heritage site. Was among those forcibly interned during WWII.

records.title: Kuni Mukai
records.description: Designed and installed the formal Japanese stroll garden at Mukai Farm in the 1930s -- the only known Japanese garden of that era designed by a woman. Self-exiled to Oregon with the family during WWII to avoid internment. Returned to Vashon after the war and resumed farming.

records.title: Masahiro (Masa) Mukai
records.description: Because his parents could not own land under Washington's 1921 Alien Land Law, the family purchased 40 acres in Masa's name in 1926. Designed the cold-process fruit barreling plant as a teenager. Received advance warning of internment from a military friend and moved his family to eastern Oregon, making them the only Vashon Japanese Americans to avoid the concentration camps. Invented his own seed harvester in Oregon. Returned to Vashon after the war.
records.period: Born 1911 on Vashon Island; active through 1990s

records.title: Deb Harrington
records.description: Constructed the Mukai Cold Process Fruit Barreling Plant in 1926, a one-story wood-frame building designed by young Masahiro Mukai. The plant is now a King County landmark and National Register site.

records.title: Melissa Jaynes
records.description: Crowned Vashon's first Strawberry Queen in 1923 at the age of 101, during the annual Strawberry Festival that celebrated the island's booming berry industry.

records.title: Lewis Cass Beall Sr
records.description: Founded the Harrington-Beall Greenhouse Company on a 23-acre site southeast of Vashon's business center. The business grew into the nation's largest grower of roses and an orchid establishment of international renown, operating for 101 years.

records.title: Tom Beall Jr
records.description: Partnered in the Harrington-Beall Greenhouse Company, growing it into a 150,000-square-foot operation with over 50 greenhouses. By 1923, it was the island's largest employer with 25 to 30 year-round workers. During WWII, rare orchids from England were shipped to the Vashon greenhouses for safekeeping.

records.title: Charles A. Cook
records.description: Platted the Magnolia Beach resort community on Vashon Island in 1902, part of the island's flourishing summer tourism industry that drew over 8,000 visitors per season from Tacoma by 1915.

records.title: G.A. Collins
records.description: Built a steam electric generating plant at Ellisport, bringing the first electric lights to Vashon Island. The system was inaugurated on November 24, 1913, with Governor Ernest Lister pressing the button.

records.title: Ernest Lister
records.description: Inaugurated the Vashon Island electrical system on November 24, 1913, by pressing the button that activated G.A. Collins's steam electric plant at Ellisport.

records.title: Ruth A. Brown
records.description: Founded Camp Sealth in 1920, the first permanent resident camp for girls in Washington State. The camp began on Blake Island and moved to a 150-acre site on Vashon Island's southwest corner in 1921. It has operated for over 100 continuous summers and expanded to nearly 400 acres.

records.title: Louis Modaranga
records.description: Attacked on the night of May 12, 1930, by four white men while employed at the Steen Mill box factory in Ellisport. Despite testimony that the assault was provoked, Modaranga was charged with felony assault while none of his attackers were arrested. His case exemplified the anti-Filipino violence faced by farmworkers during the Great Depression.

records.title: Oliver Scott Van Olinda (also Oliver Van Olinda)
records.description: Became the community's first historian, documenting early island life and settlement patterns. Taught stenography and typing on the founding faculty of Vashon College and also edited the weekly Vashon Island Press. Described the first automobiles arriving on the island in 1907 as "the most powerful influence" on island life alongside the telephone.

records.title: Heisuke Matsuda
records.description: Farmed strawberries on Vashon Island with his wife Mitsuno. Father of Mary Matsuda Gruenewald and Yoneichi Matsuda. Forcibly removed from the island on May 16, 1942, and sent to internment camps.

records.title: Mitsuno Matsuda
records.description: Strawberry farmer on Vashon Island. Mother of Mary Matsuda Gruenewald and Yoneichi Matsuda. Forcibly removed from the island and interned during WWII. Her family's story is told in her daughter's memoir "Looking Like the Enemy."

records.title: Yoneichi Matsuda
records.description: Volunteered from Heart Mountain internment camp to serve in the U.S. Army's 442nd Regimental Combat Team, the most decorated unit for its size and length of service in U.S. military history. His family had farmed strawberries on Vashon Island since 1927.

records.title: Mary Matsuda Gruenewald
records.description: Published "Looking Like the Enemy: My Story of Imprisonment in Japanese American Internment Camps" in 2005 at age 80, preserving the story of Vashon's Japanese American community. Enrolled in the U.S. Cadet Nurse Corps during the war. In 2017, Vashon Island High School retroactively awarded her the diploma she was denied when internment cut short her education.

records.title: Chiyeko Mukai
records.description: Self-exiled with her husband Masa from Vashon to Dead Ox Flat, Oregon, in March 1942 to avoid internment, as she had relatives in eastern Oregon. One of only four Mukai family members who avoided the concentration camps.

records.title: Milton Mukai
records.description: Accompanied his parents and grandmother Kuni when the Mukai family self-exiled from Vashon Island to Dead Ox Flat, Oregon, in March 1942. One of the four Mukai family members who avoided internment.

records.title: John Cherberg
records.description: Made the procedural ruling on March 12, 1959, that effectively killed the most serious Vashon Island bridge proposal in history. Ruled that the House bill had broadened the original scope and must return to committee. A vote to override his ruling failed 21 to 28, and the bridge was never built.

records.title: Fred Eernisse
records.description: Co-founded the Vashon Arts League in 1949 with Norman Edson and Art Hansen, which became the oldest private nonprofit community arts organization in Washington State. The organization eventually grew into Vashon Center for the Arts.

records.title: Norman Edson
records.description: Co-founded the Vashon Arts League in 1949, showing art created by islanders. The organization received 501(c)(3) status in 1966 and became the island's largest nonprofit arts institution.

records.title: Art Hansen
records.description: Co-founded the Vashon Arts League in 1949 with Fred Eernisse and Norman Edson, establishing the institutional foundation for the island's arts community.

records.title: Shirley Speidel
records.description: Helped revitalize the Vashon arts organization, finding a permanent home in the old Boy Scout Cabin at Ober Park. Instrumental in the organization receiving its 501(c)(3) nonprofit status in 1966 as Vashon Associated Arts.

records.title: Tony Grant
records.description: A 17-year-old who was held down by three loggers who forcibly cut his hair during the cultural tensions surrounding the counterculture influx to Vashon Island around 1970. The incident exemplified the friction between long-time residents and the incoming counterculture movement.

records.title: Bill Kirschner
records.description: University of Washington engineering graduate who pioneered fiberglass ski technology. Experimented in his grandfather Otto's garage on Vashon Island before perfecting a wet-wrap fiberglass process in 1961. Co-founded K2 Corporation with his brother Don in 1962. The company became the island's largest private employer with approximately 750 workers at its peak.

records.title: Don Kirschner
records.description: Co-founded K2 Corporation on Vashon Island with his brother Bill in 1962, named for both the world's second-highest mountain and the two Kirschner brothers. The company revolutionized the ski industry with fiberglass technology.

records.title: Otto Kirschner
records.description: His garage on Vashon Island served as the original workshop where Bill Kirschner experimented with fiberglass ski prototypes in the 1950s, leading to the founding of K2 Corporation.

records.title: Jim Stewart
records.description: Moved his coffee roasting operation to Vashon Island in 1982, purchasing a historic building in the town of Vashon. After winning a regional tasting competition, the company changed its name from Stewart Brothers Coffee to Seattle's Best Coffee. Starbucks acquired SBC in 2003 and closed the Vashon facility. The building was later reopened as The Vashon Island Coffee Roasterie.

records.title: Lawrence Matsuda
records.description: Collaborated with artist Roger Shimomura on the "Nisei Trilogy," a collaborative artwork depicting the Japanese American wartime experience, which is on permanent display in the Mukai house on Vashon Island.

records.title: Roger Shimomura
records.description: Collaborated with poet Lawrence Matsuda on the "Nisei Trilogy," a collaborative artwork depicting the Japanese American wartime experience, on permanent display at Mukai Farm and Garden on Vashon Island.

records.title: Berkeley Breathed
records.description: Wrote the children's book "Red Ranger Came Calling," inspired by Vashon Island's iconic "Bike in the Tree" landmark -- a bicycle gradually absorbed by a growing fir tree since the 1950s.

records.title: Don Puz
records.description: Original owner of the red bicycle that became the iconic "Bike in the Tree" landmark. After a devastating house fire killed his father in 1954, neighbors donated the bicycle to young Don. He left it leaning against a small fir tree, which gradually grew around it over the decades.

records.title: Jeff Ammon
records.description: Maintained the "Bike in the Tree" landmark by replacing handlebars and wheels when vandals stripped them, helping preserve one of the island's most quirky and beloved attractions.

records.title: Sharon Nelson
records.description: Founded Preserve Our Islands, the grassroots organization that led the 13-year fight against Glacier Northwest's proposed gravel mine expansion on Maury Island. The battle ended in 2010 when King County purchased the 200-acre site for $36 million, creating a new county park.

records.title: Dow Constantine
records.description: Completed the purchase of the Glacier Northwest gravel mine site on Maury Island on December 30, 2010, for $36 million. The 200-acre parcel became a county park, protecting a mile of shoreline and over 200 acres of madrone forest.

records.title: Jim Bristow
records.description: Led the Vashon Medical Reserve Corps (VMRC) in a volunteer-driven pandemic response that achieved the lowest COVID-19 case rate in King County. The program delivered over 19,000 vaccine doses, conducted 7,500+ PCR tests, and was recognized by the New York Times as a model for rural communities.

records.title: Glacial Origins
records.description: Vashon Island was formed by the retreat of the Vashon Stade of the Fraser Glaciation, the last major ice age in the Puget Sound region (~12,000–10,000 BCE). The island's terrain is composed of glacial till — a mix of clay, sand, gravel, and boulders deposited by the retreating ice sheet. The glaciation carved the deep waterways of Puget Sound that now surround the island.

records.title: Puget Sound Formation
records.description: By approximately 14,000 BCE, glacial retreat opened the Strait of Juan de Fuca, allowing saltwater to re-enter the Puget Sound basin and transforming freshwater proglacial lakes (including Glacial Lake Russell) into a saltwater inland sea. The resulting fjord system averages 450 feet in depth, with a maximum of 930 feet off Jefferson Point. Deep channels surrounding Vashon Island — some as deep as the island is high (over 600 feet) — were carved by subglacial meltwater during the Vashon Stade.

records.title: Terrain
records.description: - **Bluffs:** Steep glacial bluffs line much of the coastline, particularly on the western and northern shores. records.title: Holocene Climatic Optimum
records.description: (~7,500–2,500 BCE) A prolonged warm period with temperatures averaging ~2°C warmer than the modern baseline and ~45% less precipitation. This expanded prairie-like openings and oak woodland at the expense of dense conifer forest, influenced fire regimes, and affected distribution of plant foods important to early inhabitants. The modern cool, wet climate pattern became established after ~4,200 years ago.
